name: DEWINE, J.
description: Concurred, arguing that Ohio's non-spousal artificial insemination statute does not apply to unmarried couples and that U.S. Supreme Court precedent does not empower courts to retroactively rewrite the statute to include them or to conduct a "would have been married" inquiry.

name: BRUNNER, J.
description: Concurred in judgment only, arguing that the First District erred by considering an unpreserved issue and the Supreme Court should have reversed on that procedural ground without reaching the merits of the appeal.

name: DEWINE, J.
description: Concurred, arguing that the Ohio Constitution's command to pay compensation for taken property applies regardless of whether the property is within the taking municipality's boundaries, thus granting standing for an inverse-condemnation claim.

name: DEWINE, J.
description: Concurred, authored the opinion of the court, arguing that police officers can be victims under Marsy's Law, and therefore their identifying information can be redacted from public records.

name: FISCHER, J.
description: Concurred in part and dissented in part, arguing that officers can be victims under Marsy's Law and their information can be redacted, but the Dispatch is entitled to other unredacted footage from officers not deemed victims and that the court should have applied statutes in effect at the time of the public-records request.

name: BRUNNER, J.
description: Concurred in part and dissented in part, arguing that police officers can be victims but that the Ohio Constitution guarantees a right to access government information, and R.C. 2930.07 is unconstitutional as applied, requiring unredacted footage of police officers in public duty.

name: MENTEL, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the noneconomic damages cap in R.C. 2323.43 is unconstitutional as applied to the plaintiff's case, violating her rights to due process and equal protection.

name: DEWINE, J.
description: Concurred, authored the opinion of the court, arguing that Martens lacked standing because the Sheward public-right doctrine was an aberration that should be overruled, and he failed to establish taxpayer standing.

name: BRUNNER, J.
description: Concurred in judgment only, arguing that Martens lacked standing but that overruling the Sheward public-right doctrine was unnecessary and procedurally inappropriate in this case.

name: FISCHER, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the court should have ordered supplemental briefing on the adversity issue, but on the merits, R.C. 3705.15 only permits corrections for errors at the time of birth, not for changes arising after birth, thus affirming the lower court's denial.

name: DONNELLY, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the court should have reached the merits of the case and affirmed the lower court's decision because R.C. 3705.15 does not permit correcting a sex marker on a birth certificate for a transgender person based on changes after birth.

name: BRUNNER, J.
description: Dissented, argued that R.C. 3705.15's plain language confers authority on probate courts to correct a sex marker on any person's birth record, including for transgender individuals, and that denying such applications is unconstitutional discrimination.

name: DETERS, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the appeal lacked adversity because no other party had a legal interest that would be diminished by granting the application, and therefore the court of appeals lacked judicial power to decide the appeal.

name: DEWINE, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the Ohio Constitution's open courts provision mandates individualized balancing for sealing juvenile records, rendering the blanket sealing statute unconstitutional.

name: DONNELLY, J.
description: Concurred in judgment only, argued that the majority's analysis was unnecessarily broad and contained erroneous legal conclusions, but agreed with the final outcome.

name: STEWART, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the Enquirer had no clear right to the records as the statute mandated sealing, and the majority's novel interpretation was flawed and judicially activist.

name: KENNEDY, C.J.
description: Concurred, argued that the same-juror rule applies in all negligence cases where sequential interrogatories separate elements of negligence, requiring the same three-fourths of jurors to concur on all elements for a valid verdict.

name: BRUNNER, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the majority's application of the same-juror rule to negligence and proximate cause questions upends precedent and erodes the right to a full jury trial, and that the 'any-majority rule' should apply to non-apportionment questions.

name: FISCHER, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the proposed Ohio Citizens Redistricting Commission would be "required" to gerrymander district boundaries under the proposed constitutional amendment, and the use of "required" was not an abuse of discretion.

name: DONNELLY, J.
description: Concurred in the limited writ granted by the majority but dissented from the majority's overall opinion, arguing that the ballot language as a whole was misleading and persuasive against the amendment, requiring more extensive revisions.

name: STEWART, J.
description: Concurred in the limited writ granted by the majority but dissented from the majority's overall opinion, arguing that the ballot language as a whole was misleading and persuasive against the amendment, requiring more extensive revisions.

name: BRUNNER, J.
description: Concurred in the mandamus relief but dissented from the rest of the majority opinion, arguing that the ballot board placed partisan interests above its duties, and the court failed to require a nearly complete redrafting of the misleading and argumentative ballot language.

name: DEWINE, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the trial court erred by allowing remote testimony without sufficient case-specific findings of necessity, but this error was harmless given the overwhelming evidence of guilt.

name: FISCHER, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the trial court erred by allowing remote testimony but the error was harmless, and separately argued that the court should revisit its precedent of interpreting the Ohio Constitution's Confrontation Clause in lockstep with the Sixth Amendment.

name: Kennedy, C.J.
description: Concurred, argued that discretionary immunity is a jurisdictional bar, meaning the Court of Claims lacks subject-matter jurisdiction when it applies, and remanded the case to determine if it applies to Ohio State.

name: Brunner, J.
description: Dissented, argued that discretionary immunity is not a jurisdictional bar but an affirmative defense, and the Court of Claims should determine immunity.

name: Donnelly, J.

name: Stewart, J.

name: DeWine, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the General Assembly's temporary law allowing municipalities to tax nonresidents for work performed outside city limits during the pandemic was constitutional and a valid exercise of state legislative power, surviving rational-basis review.

name: Kennedy, C.J.
description: Dissented, argued that Section 29, as interpreted by the majority, is unconstitutional because it allows extraterritorial taxation, which violates the Home Rule Amendment by commandeering municipal taxing authority rather than merely limiting it.

name: Fischer, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the law violates the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment because it lacks a minimum connection between the taxing municipality and the nonresident taxpayer, and federal due process principles should apply to municipal taxation.

name: Fischer, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the medical-claim statute of repose clearly and unambiguously includes wrongful-death claims based on medical care, and nothing in the wrongful-death chapter negates their inclusion.

name: Donnelly, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the statutory language does not support the majority's conclusion that the medical-malpractice statute of repose applies to wrongful-death claims, and that the General Assembly has not explicitly included wrongful death among the claims listed.

name: Stewart, J.
description: Dissented, concurred with Donnelly's dissenting opinion.

name: Brunner, J.
description: Dissented, argued that applying the medical-malpractice statute of repose to wrongful-death claims unconstitutionally closes the courthouse to litigants and that wrongful-death claims are fundamentally different from medical malpractice claims.

name: DEWINE, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the Power Siting Board's orders granting certificates for solar farms were lawful and reasonable, as the citizens failed to establish otherwise.

name: BRUNNER, J.
description: Concurred in part and in the judgment, argued that the majority opinion improperly and unnecessarily discussed the TWISM case regarding agency deference, as it was not relevant to the factual issues presented.

name: STEWART, J.

name: DEWINE, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the arson-offender registration is not part of a criminal sentence and the legislature can limit judicial discretion, thus no separation-of-powers violation.

name: STEWART, J.
description: Concurred, argued that while the statute is constitutional, it is poorly drafted, lacks guidance, and is prone to abuse and equal-protection challenges.

name: BRUNNER, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the statute unconstitutionally allows the executive branch to control judicial discretion over sentencing, violating separation of powers.

name: DONNELLY, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the statute unconstitutionally allows the executive branch to control judicial discretion over sentencing, violating separation of powers.

name: FISCHER, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the statute violates separation of powers by letting the executive branch determine if a court can exercise discretion in reducing registration periods.

name: Donnelly, J.
description: Concurred, argued that while advocacy seemed to infiltrate the ballot language process, voters would still be fully informed.

name: Stewart, J.
description: Concurred in part and dissented in part, argued that the ballot board failed its constitutional duty by crafting partisan and misleading language, and the full text of the amendment should have been used.

name: Brunner, J.
description: Concurred in part and dissented in part, argued that the ballot board majority shirked its responsibility, obfuscated the amendment's language with deceit and bias, and created misleading language to influence the election outcome, advocating for the full text.

name: Deters, J.
description: Concurred in part and dissented in part, argued that the term "citizens of the State" is not misleading and the ballot language does not deceive voters, disagreeing with the majority's finding on this specific point.

name: Kennedy, C.J.
description: Concurred, argued that concurred with Deters, J.'s opinion.

name: DeWine, J.
description: Concurred, argued that concurred with Deters, J.'s opinion.

name: Deters, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the Reagan Tokes Law is constitutional and does not violate separation of powers, the right to a jury trial, or procedural due process.

name: Brunner, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the Reagan Tokes Law facially violates offenders' rights to procedural due process due to insufficient procedures and should be invalidated.

name: Donnelly, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the Reagan Tokes Law facially violates offenders' rights to procedural due process due to insufficient procedures and should be invalidated.

name: Fischer, J.
description: Concurred in judgment only, agreeing with the outcome but not necessarily all the reasoning.

name: Donnelly, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the General Assembly is bound by its own laws regarding special election dates and cannot use a joint resolution to violate those laws, making the August 8 election unlawful.

name: Stewart
description: Dissented, concurred with Justice Donnelly's opinion, arguing the General Assembly cannot repeal or invalidate statutes by joint resolution.

name: Brunner, J.
description: Dissented, joined Justice Donnelly's opinion and separately argued that the majority's interpretation of "prescribe" is harmful, allowing the General Assembly to violate its own laws and undermining democratic norms.

name: DONNELLY, J.
description: Concurred with the majority's mandated changes but dissented regarding the word "elevating" in the ballot title, arguing it is prejudicial and should be changed to a neutral word.

name: STEWART, J.
description: Concurred in part and dissented in part, joining Judge Donnelly's opinion.

name: BRUNNER, J.
description: Concurred with the majority's mandated changes but dissented, arguing the ballot language should more clearly explain the different standards for citizen-initiated versus General Assembly amendments to avoid obfuscating a fundamental shift in power.

name: Kennedy, C.J.
description: Concurred in judgment, argued that the court's precedent improperly imposed a "single-subject rule" on the people's power to propose constitutional amendments, but agreed the petition was a single amendment.

name: Fischer, J.
description: Concurred in judgment with majority opinion.

name: Kennedy, C.J.
description: Concurred in judgment only in part and dissented in part, argued that the majority erred by concluding that judges' oaths of office are governed by the Rules of Superintendence rather than the Public Records Act, and that the court lacks constitutional authority to preempt substantive law.

name: DeWine, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the majority erred by concluding that judges' oaths of office are governed by the Rules of Superintendence rather than the Public Records Act, and that the court lacks constitutional authority to preempt substantive law.

name: O'Connor, C.J.
description: Concurred, argued that R.C. 2315.18 is unconstitutional as applied to Brandt because it arbitrarily excludes severe psychological injuries from its exceptions, violating the due-course-of-law guarantee.

name: Kennedy, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the majority opinion overreaches judicial authority by substituting its policy preferences for the General Assembly's legislative decisions and that Brandt failed to prove the statute was unconstitutional as applied.

name: Fischer, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the majority opinion abandons the court's impartial role and exceeds its authority by striking down the caps, and that Brandt failed to demonstrate the statute was unconstitutional on its face or as applied.

name: DeWine, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the majority opinion overreaches judicial authority by substituting its policy preferences for the General Assembly's legislative decisions and that Brandt failed to prove the statute was unconstitutional as applied.

name: STEWART, J.
description: Concurred, argued that a constitutional right to a jury trial does not attach to a wrongful-imprisonment action against the state because this type of action did not exist at common law.

name: DEWINE, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the claim for a jury trial fails due to the lack of a historical analogue and because it is inconsistent with the state's limited waiver of sovereign immunity.

name: DONNELLY, J.
description: Dissented, argued that a constitutional right to a jury trial exists in an action under R.C. 2743.48 to be declared a wrongfully imprisoned person.

name: BRUNNER
description: Concurred, argued that victims had a right to restitution under Marsy's Law but forfeited it by not appealing the initial denial, and the trial court lost jurisdiction after the sentence became final.

name: O'Connor
description: Concurred, argued that the trial court lacked jurisdiction to modify Brasher's sentence solely because the Double Jeopardy Clause prohibited imposing restitution after the sentence was completed.

name: DeWine
description: Concurred, argued that the trial court erred for two independent reasons: lack of jurisdiction after final judgment and expired appeal time, and violation of Double Jeopardy due to Brasher's legitimate expectation of finality.

name: Stewart, J.
description: Concurred, argued that Morris's life sentence without considering his youth as a mitigating factor constitutes cruel and unusual punishment under both Ohio and federal constitutions, consistent with *State v. Patrick*.

name: FISCHER, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the majority incorrectly reaffirms *State v. Patrick* which was overruled by *Jones v. Mississippi* on federal law, and that the Ohio Constitution does not independently require on-the-record consideration of youth.

name: KENNEDY
description: Dissented, argued that while youth must be considered, the Eighth Amendment does not require courts to expressly consider a juvenile's age on the record, and *State v. Patrick* should be overruled on that point.

name: DeWINE, J.
description: Dissented, argued that while youth must be considered, the Eighth Amendment does not require courts to expressly consider a juvenile's age on the record, and *State v. Patrick* should be overruled on that point.

name: Brunner, J.
description: Concurred, argued that R.C. 2152.84(A)(2)(b) is fundamentally unfair as applied to D.R. because it removes judicial discretion at a critical stage, violating due process.

name: Fischer, J.
description: Dissented, argued that R.C. 2152.84 complies with due process because no existing protected substantive right is at stake at the completion-of-disposition stage.

name: DeWine, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the majority misinterprets procedural due process and that the law requiring sex offender registration for 16- and 17-year-olds is constitutional.

name: Kennedy, J.
description: Concurred with Justice DeWine's dissenting opinion.

name: Brunner, J.
description: Concurred, argued that a criminal defendant has a constitutional and statutory right to a bill of particulars upon timely request, and the state's failure to provide one, despite open-file discovery, prejudiced the defendant's ability to prepare a defense.

name: FISCHER, J.
description: Concurred, but only with the judgment, implying a different reasoning than the majority.

name: DeWine, J.
description: Dissented, argued that Haynes forfeited his argument by changing it on appeal and that he suffered no prejudice because all necessary information was available through open-file discovery.

name: Kennedy, J.
description: Dissented, argued that Haynes forfeited his argument and suffered no prejudice from the lack of a bill of particulars due to open-file discovery.

name: Brunner, J.
description: Concurred, argued that Marsy's Law provides a right to "full and timely restitution" but did not alter the meaning of "restitution" in Ohio law, which is limited to economic losses directly and proximately caused by the offense, thus excluding lost wages for court attendance.

name: DeWine, J.
description: Dissented, argued that Ohio voters approved Marsy's Law to significantly expand victims' rights, including the right to "full and timely restitution," and that lost wages due to court attendance are a foreseeable consequence of the crime and should be compensable.

name: Donnelly, J.
description: Dissented from granting the writ of mandamus, arguing that R.C. 731.31 should apply to charter-amendment petitions, making the relators' petition deficient.

name: Brunner, J.
description: Dissented, arguing that Hackworth was correctly decided and R.C. 731.31 should apply, thus the petition was deficient.

name: Brunner, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the March 2 plan is unlawful, the respondents' abuse of legislative privilege is unjustifiable, and the dissenting opinion's position on maximizing competitive seats is not supported by the record.

name: Kennedy, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the March 2 plan is constitutional as it does not excessively split counties and reasonably attempts to maximize competitive seats, and that the majority wrongly applies a proportionality standard not found in Article XIX.

name: DeWine, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the March 2 plan is constitutional as it does not excessively split counties and reasonably attempts to maximize competitive seats, and that the majority wrongly applies a proportionality standard not found in Article XIX.

name: Fischer, J.
description: Dissented, argued that petitioners failed to prove their case beyond a reasonable doubt and that the court's expedited procedure was fundamentally flawed, leading to an uninformed decision.

name: Kennedy, J.
description: Dissented, argued that neither group of relators had a clear legal right to relief as the federal court order did not extend filing deadlines, and the majority's decision was an exercise of raw political power that disrupted the election process.

name: Fischer, J.
description: Dissented, argued that neither group of relators had a clear legal right to relief, joining Justice Kennedy's opinion and emphasizing the chaos caused by the court's redistricting decisions.

name: DeWine, J.
description: Dissented, argued that neither the court nor the Secretary of State had authority to alter legislative filing deadlines, and the federal court order did not implicitly move these deadlines, leading to disruption and unconstitutional action.

name: Kennedy, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the Ohio Constitution grants the General Assembly spending power and authority to establish courts, and the challenged statutes do not infringe on municipal home-rule authority.

name: Fischer, J.
description: Concurred, argued that Ohio's jurisprudence on standby and hybrid representation needs reevaluation due to the practical difficulties faced by standby counsel in capital cases, and that the Ohio Constitution supports a right to hybrid representation.

name: BRUNNER, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the restriction on transferability in the deed is valid, reasonable, and serves a charitable or public purpose, and that the transfer of mineral interests violated these deed restrictions.

name: Donnelly, J.
description: Concurred, argued that CDC violated enforceable land-transfer restrictions and OPWC was entitled to remedies, but did not join the part of the opinion regarding the enforceability of use restrictions as that issue was not raised.

name: DeWine, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the Transfer Restriction is an invalid restraint on alienation under both traditional common-law and modern reasonableness approaches, and the court should have reinstated the trial court's judgment.

name: Kennedy, J.

name: Donnelly, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the congressional-district plan is unconstitutional due to undue partisan favoritism and splitting of governmental units, violating Article XIX.

name: Brunner, J.
description: Concurred with the majority opinion and joined Chief Justice O'Connor's concurring opinion.

name: O'Connor, C.J.
description: Concurred, argued that the evidence overwhelmingly demonstrates a partisan advantage for the Republican Party and that the respondents' 'competitiveness' standard is an illusion.

name: Kennedy, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the majority's decision lacks a workable standard for 'undue' favoritism or splitting, and improperly uses a proportional representation standard not mandated by the Constitution.

name: Donnelly, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the trial court's bail was set at an unaffordable level, making it excessive and effectively a denial of bail, and that the dissent misinterprets the issue.

name: Kennedy, J.
description: Dissented, argued that DuBose failed to prove the trial court abused its discretion in setting bail, and that the $1,500,000 bail was valid given evidence of flight risk and threat to the victim's family.

name: Fischer, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the abuse-of-discretion standard of review should have been applied, not de novo review, when the appellate court only reviewed existing evidence.

name: DeWine, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the majority's decision makes communities less safe by applying the wrong standard of review, disregarding victims' rights, and prohibiting courts from considering public safety in setting bail.

name: Stewart, J.
description: Concurred, argued that a municipality may acquire excess electricity for reasons other than solely for extraterritorial resale, but cannot acquire it solely for that purpose, and remanded the case for factual determination.

name: Donnelly, J.
description: Concurred, but agreed only with the judgment to remand the case.

name: DeWine, J.
description: Concurred in part and dissented in part, argued that a municipality may only sell excess electricity it has produced, not purchased, and that purchasing electricity solely for extraterritorial resale is unconstitutional.

name: Kennedy, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the Ohio Constitution expressly permits municipalities to sell surplus electricity extraterritorially, regardless of whether the surplus is "artificial," and would have reinstated summary judgment for the city.

name: Brunner, J.
description: Dissented, argued that while municipalities can acquire surplus electricity for lawful reasons, the facts do not support overturning summary judgment for the city based on Toledo Edison Co., and would have reversed the appellate court.

name: O'Connor, C.J.
description: Concurred, argued that a writ of prohibition was warranted because Judge Peeler's order restoring firearms rights was unauthorized by law and Suwalski, as a crime victim, had the right to challenge it under Marsy's Law.

name: Kennedy, J.
description: Dissented, argued that Marsy's Law rights asserted by Suwalski were not implicated in the relief-from-disability matter, and therefore she lacked standing to bring the prohibition action.

name: O'Connor, C.J.
description: Concurred, argued that a warrantless public arrest based on probable cause is constitutional and does not require exigent circumstances or impracticability of obtaining a warrant.

name: Stewart, J.
description: Dissented, argued that law enforcement officers acted outside their statutory authority by making a warrantless arrest when they had ample time to secure a warrant, violating Article I, Section 14 of the Ohio Constitution.

name: Brunner, J.
description: Dissented, argued that law enforcement officers acted outside their statutory authority by making a warrantless arrest when they had ample time to secure a warrant, violating Article I, Section 14 of the Ohio Constitution.

name: KENNEDY, J.
description: Concurred, argued that Sierah's Law is remedial and its retroactive application does not violate the Ohio Constitution's Retroactivity Clause.

name: STEWART, J.
description: Dissented, argued that Sierah's Law is punitive and its retroactive application violates the Ohio Constitution's Retroactivity Clause.

name: DONNELLY, J.
description: Dissented, argued that Sierah's Law is punitive and its retroactive application violates the Ohio Constitution's Retroactivity Clause.
